intro: Thérèse Dussaut plays Ravel’s 1899 piano original, with its long melody above evenly spaced accompanying chords. How does the tune stretch across that regular pulse?
question: How can a melody float above a steady dance pulse?

cues.title: A line above the chords
cues.text: The opening melody stretches across the regular accompanying chords. Listen for the independence of those two rhythms: a long melodic note can continue while the harmony beneath it takes another step.
cues.evidence: The piano score gives the melody longer values above a regular accompaniment; no individual note is aligned to the recording.
cues.how: A general description of this stretch of music.

cues.title: Fauré and a patron’s salon
cues.text: Ravel wrote the Pavane in 1899 while studying with Fauré. His teacher introduced him to the salon of the Princesse de Polignac, the work’s dedicatee.
cues.evidence: Bru Zane’s work note records the composition year, Fauré’s introduction and the dedication.

cues.title: Let the phrase release
cues.text: Through the first contrasting episode, follow how the phrase expands and then releases. The piano’s decay matters between attacks: reducing a chord’s weight need not mean abandoning the underlying dance pulse.
cues.evidence: The analysis shows a pronounced relative-level fall around 1:10–1:15 within the first contrasting span.

cues.title: The returning refrain
cues.text: The opening melody serves as a refrain between contrasting episodes. Around its return, compare the lengths of the phrases with the first statement: familiarity gives the ear a reference point without making the intervening music redundant.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the refrain’s return; an audio change near 1:54 supports approximate placement rather than a verified melodic onset.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: An imagined Spanish court
cues.text: The title does not commemorate a particular dead princess. Ravel described an imagined pavane that a princess might have danced at the Spanish court in earlier centuries, rather than a funeral lament.
cues.evidence: Bru Zane and Herbert Glass’s LA Phil note quote Ravel’s explanation of the title and character.

cues.title: The broader contrasting episode
cues.text: The later contrasting episode builds stronger phrases than the opening refrain. Keep the upper melody distinct from the chordal weight beneath it; the measured pace leaves room to follow both.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the contrasting episode; changes around 2:44–2:52 precede stronger relative-level peaks near 3:10.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Expansion and release
cues.text: Within this broader episode, listen to the shape of successive rises and withdrawals. A stronger chord is part of a phrase, not necessarily its destination; keep following the upper line after each peak.
cues.evidence: The relative-level peak near 3:10 is followed by a withdrawal around 3:20 and further peaks around 3:45–3:50.

cues.title: The last refrain
cues.text: The final refrain carries the piece towards its close after the broader episode. Compare the familiar melody’s scale with the larger intervening phrases, rather than treating its return as a completely new beginning.
cues.evidence: The score places the refrain last; the low-level interval around 4:00 supports its approximate position in the recording.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: From piano to orchestra
cues.text: Ricardo Viñes gave the piano premiere on 5 April 1902 at the Société nationale de musique. Ravel made his orchestral version in 1910; this recording uses the earlier piano version.
cues.evidence: Bru Zane’s work note records Viñes’s premiere and the 1910 orchestration; the recording source identifies a piano performance.

cues.title: The closing resonance
cues.text: The closing passage settles into G major and leaves the piano’s resonance to diminish. Listen through that decay rather than treating the last chord’s attack as the whole ending.
cues.evidence: The score supplies the final key; the analysis shows a substantial relative-level decline and no detected new attacks in the last window.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: A moving bass gives way to low B
transitions.how: The refrain broadens towards its close, then Ravel restores the original pace and marks the new episode “Très lointain” — very distant. Low B octaves anchor B-minor colouring beneath a melody carried in closely spaced chords. The piano’s moving bass has become a held foundation, while the upper parts acquire a more uniform rhythmic shape. The B-minor chord shares B and D with G major, so the shift of bass and texture announces the contrast before further chromatic inflections accumulate.
transitions.evidence: The first-episode marker is 0:48, a strong measured boundary followed by B-minor estimates. The original piano score, pp. 1–2, shows the broadening, restored tempo, “Très lointain” instruction, low B octaves and chordal line: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP384819-PMLP03577-Maurice_Ravel_-_Pavane_pour_une_infante_d%C3%A9funte.pdf. No orchestral horn is assigned to this piano performance.

transitions.title: A held chord interrupts the harmonic sliding
transitions.how: The episode’s closing phrases move through chromatic chord shapes, including parallel dominant ninths, rather than relying only on a single dominant chord aimed at home. Ravel broadens the motion and holds the last sonority under a fermata. “Reprenez le mouvement” then restores the refrain’s pace and G-major frame. The familiar long melody floats above repeated accompanying attacks again, but fuller low chords replace the opening’s lighter bass writing: return is recognisable without being an exact copy.
transitions.evidence: The first-return boundary is 1:54, a measured change. The provisional relation matches 0:21–0:46.5 with 2:11.5–2:37. The piano score, pp. 2–3, supplies the chromatic closing chords, fermata and changed bass under the refrain. The dominant-ninth parallelism is independently illustrated at https://musictheory.pugetsound.edu/mt21c/Impressionism.html. The release of the fermata is not precisely aligned.

transitions.title: The large chord releases a quieter line
transitions.how: The refrain reaches a forceful, broadened close, then the next idea begins “subitement très doux et très lié” — suddenly very soft and very connected. Ravel turns away from the G-major refrain’s pitch collection through B♭ and other chromatic inflections, rather than presenting another plain tonic statement. The bass initially leaves more space, and the upper line acquires flowing connective notes. This soft entrance is the start of the broader episode, not its climax: stronger chordal writing grows from it later.
transitions.evidence: The broader-episode boundary is 2:44, near strong measured changes at 2:44 and 2:52. The score, pp. 3–4, shows the Large close, restored movement, sudden soft instruction and flatter upper-line inflections before the later crescendos. The audio’s fluctuating key estimates are not treated as proof of one new tonic.

transitions.title: A shortened bar holds back the last return
transitions.how: The broader episode descends through chromatic chords and loses weight. Ravel marks the end “Très grave”, shortens the metre to 2/4 and places a fermata over the final chord: the normal four-beat span is interrupted before the refrain resumes. G major and the original melodic contour return with the regular pulse, now above a more flowing accompaniment. The bass and familiar phrase shape restore orientation after the sliding harmony, while the moving inner notes prevent the last return from sounding merely repeated.
transitions.evidence: The final-return marker is 4:04, after the low-level interval around 4:00 and a measured change at 3:56. The piano score, pp. 4–5, supplies the chromatic descent, Très grave, short bar, fermata and altered accompaniment. The provisional relation matches 1:54.5–2:22 with 4:06.5–4:34, supporting thematic return rather than a literal replay of every layer.

composer.background:
Ravel was born in Ciboure, across the harbour from Saint-Jean-de-Luz, to Marie Delouart, a Basque woman who had lived in Madrid, and Pierre-Joseph Ravel, a Swiss-born engineer. The family moved to Paris when Maurice was three months old. His father encouraged music as well as an interest in machinery; his mother’s songs gave him an early acquaintance with Spanish idioms. Basque ancestry and Spanish musical theatre remained distinct resources: the uneven pulse of the Piano Trio differs from the habanera of the Rapsodie espagnole. He returned to the Basque coast for holidays and composition, but received his musical education in Paris.

He entered the Conservatoire in 1889, initially as a pianist, and studied with Charles-Wilfrid de Bériot. Failure to win the required prizes cost him his place in 1895. Readmitted in 1897 to Fauré’s composition class, he also learnt counterpoint from André Gedalge. Fauré encouraged the individual ear without relaxing the demands of construction; Gedalge supplied the discipline behind the fugues and independent inner parts. Ravel did not become a virtuoso pianist. Ricardo Viñes, his friend since adolescence, introduced much of the difficult piano music, including Jeux d’eau, Miroirs and Gaspard de la nuit.
composer.epithet: An engineer of instrumental colour who made a piano imitate water, an orchestra imitate a machine, and old dances carry the names of the dead.
